description: Checks whether the checks a repository declares can actually fail. Plants a known defect into a copy of the file its own history shows as the most repaired, runs the repository's declared gates against it, and counts a catch only when a gate names the planted file and stays quiet on the clean one. Zero dependencies, one command.
rules: A green check proves nothing until it has been shown to go red. After adding or changing any gate, run `npx agent-quality-kit prove`: the gate must fail on its own bad sample and stay quiet on the good one. A gate that passes both proves nothing.
There are three outcomes, not two: clean, finding, and could-not-check. A gate that failed to run is not a finding about the code — fix the tooling, never the file it happened to name while dying.

Never make a check pass by weakening it: `|| true`, `--exit-zero`, `continue-on-error: true`, blanket suppressions. That turns a failure into silence, which is the exact defect this tool exists to find. If a check is wrong, stop and ask the human.

Every rule written into AGENTS.md needs a named arbiter beside it: `<!-- aqk: gate-name -->` when a machine holds it, or `<!-- aqk: human -->` when none does. The second is an honest admission; a rule with neither is a promise nobody keeps.
"Done" means an arbiter said so. Name the command that was red and is now green — `looks correct` is not done.
To decide what to fix first, run `npx agent-quality-kit prompt`: it prints at most five items ordered by weight, and every item carries the command that proves it done.

`npx agent-quality-kit doctor --run --since main` narrows findings to the files a branch touched, so inherited debt does not bury today's change. A gate that could not run is never narrowed away by it.

The kit sends nothing on its own. Its only outgoing request of its own asks npm whether a newer version exists. `aqk feedback` prints a report with no paths, no code and no repository name; `aqk feedback --send` posts that same report through the user's own `gh`, and the consent lives in the flag — without it `gh` is never called even once, and a machine check holds that.
